claims.claim: NIMH's working account: treatment for mental illnesses usually includes therapy (virtual or in person), medication, or a combination of the two, and there are ways to get help for a mental illness, emotional struggles, or mental health concerns.
The goals of mental health treatment are relief from symptoms, maintaining or enhancing daily functioning, and improving quality of life (NIMH, psychotherapies page).

Psychotherapy (talk therapy) refers to a variety of treatments that aim to help a person identify and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors; the APA Dictionary describes it as any psychological service provided by a trained professional that primarily uses forms of communication and interaction.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is a form of psychotherapy that helps clients examine how their thoughts affect their behavior and aims to change cognitive distortions and self-defeating behaviors; hundreds of studies support its effectiveness across numerous disorders (OpenStax; APA Dictionary).

Medications can play an important role in treating mental disorders and conditions and are often used in combination with other treatments, such as psychotherapy (NIMH, mental health medications page).

In group therapy — the professional form of a support group — a clinician meets together with several clients with similar problems; one documented benefit is decreasing a client's shame and isolation while offering support from the therapist and other group members (OpenStax).
A psychiatrist is a physician who specializes in the diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and study of mental, behavioral, and personality disorders (APA Dictionary).

A psychologist is professionally trained in one or more branches or subfields of psychology, with doctoral-level training, and works in a variety of settings including clinics, hospitals, schools, and private practice (APA Dictionary).

A counselor is professionally trained in counseling, psychology, social work, or nursing and specializes in one or more counseling areas, such as vocational, educational, or family counseling (APA Dictionary).

Besides psychologists and psychiatrists, clinical social workers and other trained professionals also provide counseling and therapy, and licensing requirements vary from state to state (OpenStax; NIMH lists social workers among mental health professionals).

SAMHSA defines recovery as a process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives, and strive to reach their full potential — a functioning standard, not a perfection standard.

Treatment plans are individualized: choosing the right treatment plan is based on a person's individual needs and medical situation and should occur under the guidance of a mental health professional, and it may take several tries to find what works best (NIMH).

Psychotherapy and medication are the most common forms of mental health treatment, and psychotherapy can be used as an alternative to or alongside medication and other treatment options (NIMH); OpenStax likewise frames psychotherapy and biomedical therapy as the two broad types of treatment, both of which help people with psychological disorders.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does treatment cure mental illness, or aim at recovery and functioning?
positions: Popular expectation that treatment should produce a complete cure

SAMHSA defines recovery as a process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives, and strive to reach their full potential; NIMH states treatment goals of symptom relief, maintaining or enhancing daily functioning, and improving quality of life
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the recovery framing attributed to SAMHSA and NIMH: treatment aims at recovery and functioning, not perfection. No cure claims are made, and recovery is presented as a process, not a switch.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is there one best treatment for everyone with a given condition?
positions: One-size-fits-all expectations ('the same treatment works for everyone with the same condition')

NIMH: the right treatment plan is based on a person's individual needs and medical situation and should occur under the guidance of a mental health professional; it may take several tries to find what works best
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the honest note that one size does not fit all, attributed to NIMH, and keeps all statements general (no specific treatments for specific conditions).

positions: Assumption that medication is the treatment, or that talk therapy alone is always enough

conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the combination fact generally and factually. Specific medication details (names, dosing, side effects) are out of scope and owned by the pharmacology subject.

sourceRecords.title: Psychotherapies — NIMH Health Topics
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: psychotherapy (talk therapy) as a variety of treatments aiming to help a person identify and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors; psychotherapy and medication as the most common forms of mental health treatment; goals of psychotherapy (relief from symptoms, maintaining or enhancing daily functioning, improving quality of life); CBT as an element of psychotherapy; treatment plans chosen based on individual needs under the guidance of a mental health professional; psychotherapy used as an alternative to or alongside medication. Facts synthesized in original wording; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Mental Health Medications — NIMH Health Topics
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: medications can play an important role in treating mental disorders and conditions; they are often used in combination with other treatments such as psychotherapy; it may take several tries to find the medication that works best with the fewest side effects; working with a health care provider or mental health professional on an individualized treatment plan. Used only for general, class-level statements; specific drug names and dosing details were deliberately NOT included (pharmacology owns those).

sourceRecords.title: Help for Mental Illnesses — NIMH
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the core message that there are ways to get help for a mental illness, emotional struggles, or mental health concerns; treatment for mental illnesses usually includes therapy (virtual or in person), medication, or a combination of the two; a primary care provider can perform an initial screening and refer to a mental health professional (such as a social worker, psychologist, or psychiatrist); bringing up mental health concerns with a provider and asking for help as a first step. No crisis-line content used; the lesson keeps a calm, non-scary tone.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 16.1: Mental Health Treatment: Past and Present
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/20200805171705id_/) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: there are many different types of treatment providers and licensing requirements vary from state to state; besides psychologists and psychiatrists, clinical social workers, marriage and family therapists, and other trained professionals perform counseling and therapy; voluntary versus involuntary treatment; psychological treatment occurs in a variety of places (community centers, private practice, schools, prisons). Historical treatment material (asylums, deinstitutionalization) was deliberately left out of scope. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 16.2: Types of Treatment
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/20200803182736id_/) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: psychotherapy and biomedical therapy as the two broad types of treatment, both of which help people with psychological disorders; psychotherapy as a psychological treatment employing various methods to help someone overcome personal problems or attain personal growth; biomedical therapy as involving medication and/or medical procedures; CBT helps clients examine how their thoughts affect their behavior and aims to change cognitive distortions and self-defeating behaviors; hundreds of studies support CBT's effectiveness. Medication specifics and biomedical procedure details were not used (pharmacology owns them).

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 16.3: Treatment Modalities

Supports: group therapy — a clinician meets together with several clients with similar problems; one benefit is decreasing a client's shame and isolation about a problem while offering needed support from both the therapist and other group members. sourceRecords.title: Psychotherapy — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API (getdopdefinitions endpoint). Definition: any psychological service provided by a trained professional that primarily uses forms of communication and interaction to assess, diagnose, and treat dysfunctional emotional reactions, ways of thinking, and behavior patterns; may be provided to individuals, couples, families, or groups; major categories include psychodynamic, cognitive/behavior, humanistic, and integrative therapies. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT) — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: a form of psychotherapy that integrates theories of cognition and learning with treatment techniques derived from cognitive therapy and behavior therapy; assumes cognitive, emotional, and behavioral variables are functionally interrelated; treatment aims at identifying and modifying maladaptive thought processes and problematic behaviors. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Psychiatrist — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: a physician who specializes in the diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and study of mental, behavioral, and personality disorders; U.S. training includes medical school plus a psychiatric residency. Used for the one-line provider description (physician identity, specialty). Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Psychologist — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: an individual professionally trained in one or more branches or subfields of psychology, with doctoral-level training (PhD, PsyD, or EdD), working in a variety of settings including laboratories, schools, social agencies, hospitals, clinics, and private practice. Used for the one-line provider description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Counselor — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: an individual professionally trained in counseling, psychology, social work, or nursing who specializes in one or more counseling areas, such as vocational, rehabilitation, educational, substance abuse, marriage, relationship, or family counseling; provides professional evaluations, information, and suggestions designed to enhance the client's ability to solve problems and make decisions. Used for the one-line provider description. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Group Therapy — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: treatment of psychological problems in which two or more participants interact with each other in the presence of one or more psychotherapists; approaches aim to provide an environment in which problems and concerns can be shared in an atmosphere of mutual respect and understanding. Used alongside OpenStax 16.3 for the support-group one-liner. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Recovery and Recovery Support — SAMHSA
sourceRecords.provider: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports the recovery idea: SAMHSA defines recovery as a process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives, and strive to reach their full potential; recovery signals a shift in the expectation for positive outcomes for people with mental and substance use conditions. The lesson presents recovery as a functioning standard, not a perfection standard, attributed to this definition. No statistics from this page are cited; all examples are original and fictional.
